beats.beat: Explain the business model in everyday terms: the company does not sell to the open market; it bids in tenders floated by clients, and work goes to the lowest quote through a Letter of Acceptance. The DRHP lays out the full six-step process, from tender to site handover.

Name the two segments: creation of infrastructure, and operating a ready-mix concrete (RMC) plant. The infrastructure side covers railway platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion, track laying, bridges of many types, and bituminous and concrete roads; the RMC plant is at Kashimira, Thane district, Maharashtra.

List the named customers: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, MMRDA, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation, plus private clients Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp. Western Railway has been a client since 2006.

Position the company: the DRHP calls it a major player in developing infrastructure in Mumbai, consolidating its position in Maharashtra with a strong order book, while its own SWOT flags the slow pace of government projects and a working-capital crunch as weaknesses.
Give the dependency numbers directly: Western Railway is the major client and contributes 52% of orders on hand; revenue from key customers for the year ended 31 March 2018 was 57% of total revenue.

business.heading: What the company does
business.purpose: Explain the tender-based contract model and the two operating segments before naming clients and concentration.

beats.beat: Explain the unit convention once: the restated statements are printed in lakhs; this report converts to crore by dividing by 100, so the comparisons are easy to read.

Lead the narrative with revenue, which has declined in three of the past five years: ₹86.61 crore (FY2014), ₹90.21 crore (FY2015), ₹74.53 crore (FY2016), ₹73.44 crore (FY2017), ₹60.53 crore (FY2018) — roughly a 33% fall from the FY2015 peak.
Show EBITDA, which stayed positive through the revenue slide: ₹7.84 crore (FY2014), ₹9.46 crore (FY2015), ₹7.83 crore (FY2016), ₹6.76 crore (FY2017), ₹9.29 crore (FY2018).

Present PAT as a collapse and a rebound: ₹0.96 crore (FY2014), ₹0.78 crore (FY2015), ₹0.33 crore (FY2016), ₹0.16 crore (FY2017), then a sharp ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 — a one-year jump, not a smooth trend.

Add the balance-sheet spine: total assets rose from ₹70.62 crore in FY2014 to ₹82.32 crore in FY2018; long-term borrowings are small at ₹1.33 crore in FY2018, but short-term borrowings are much larger at ₹35.37 crore in FY2018, up from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014.

Flag the liquidity warnings: the company had ₹405.02 lakh (₹4.05 crore) of unsecured loans repayable on demand as of 31 March 2018, and the DRHP says it had negative cash flow in recent financial years — the exact cash-flow figures are not in the extract.

beats.beat: Name the promoter: Amit Bholanath Mishra, sole promoter and Managing Director, holds 74,95,476 equity shares — 90.949% of the pre-issue paid-up capital. He is not a wilful defaulter, per the filing.

Describe the ownership and management picture: the director shareholding table shows Mishra with 74,95,476 shares and three whole-time directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — with 300 shares each. The CFO is Anchal Pachori, aged 28 and a chartered accountant; the company secretary is Mohit Soni, aged 26. KMP Hatim Sakerwala holds 9% of the equity.

Surface the related-party transactions: in FY2018 the company took loans of ₹68.4 lakh from KMP/board members, paid director remuneration of ₹57.7 lakh, and had ₹324.3 lakh of outstanding payables to related parties as of 31 March 2018. The risk section acknowledges past RPTs and says they may continue.

Record the litigation and integrity disclosures: no criminal cases or investigations are pending against directors, and no director or promoter is on the RBI list of wilful defaulters. But two companies promoted by the promoter — Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited — were struck off by the ROC in March 2016 for non-operation.

Note the process flags: no independent agency has appraised the proposed project and no monitoring agency has been appointed; fund deployment is at the discretion of management and the board, though monitored by the audit committee.

beats.beat: Define the sandbox: infrastructure and construction, which the DRHP describes as a highly fragmented and working-capital-intensive market contributing roughly 8% of India's GDP at constant prices, with both organised and unorganised competition.

List the demand drivers the filing leans on: government flagship programmes such as 100 Smart Cities, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All; eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including real estate and construction; and an estimated ₹50 trillion investment requirement in infrastructure by 2022.

Add the macro figures the DRHP cites: cumulative growth of eight core industries of 4.2% in 2017-18; India's GDP growth expected to stay above 7% in 2017; logistics expected to grow at 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020; working-age population to rise to 64% by 2021.
Close the section with the headwinds the company itself names: slow pace of government projects, changes in government policy, and working-capital strain that could affect profitability.

beats.beat: Open with a plain orientation: A B Infrabuild is an infrastructure contractor working largely in Mumbai and Maharashtra, and it runs two businesses — building railway, bridge and road works for government clients, and manufacturing ready-mix concrete at a Thane plant.
State the shape of the filing: a 44,28,000-equity-share SME Board issue at a price yet to be determined; the rupee size of the issue is not yet disclosed.
Set the stakes: the company earned 57% of its FY2018 revenue from Indian Railways and has Western Railway at about half its order book — a concentration that frames the whole risk section.

Name the intermediaries: Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited is the lead manager and Bigshare Services Private Limited is the registrar.
State the objects of the issue: ₹1,130.00 lakhs (₹11.30 crore) for working capital requirements; general corporate purposes is listed as the second object with an undisclosed amount.

offer.purpose: Lay out exactly what is being sold, who is running the issue, what the money is for, and what is not disclosed.

beats.beat: Customer concentration: one client, Indian Railways, contributed 57% of FY2018 revenue, and the filing warns that losing that client would cause a significant dip in revenue; Western Railway alone is 52% of the orders on hand.

Tender-dependent revenue: the company's revenues largely depend on government accepting its bid submissions; if most bids are not won or are negotiated at lower values, performance suffers — and failure to secure new government and PSU contracts would materially hurt the financial condition.

Liquidity and working-capital strain: the DRHP discloses negative cash flow in recent years, ₹4.05 crore of unsecured loans repayable on demand, and its own SWOT lists a working-capital crunch that may affect profitability.

Geographic and order-book concentration: most revenue is generated in and around Mumbai, so adverse developments there hurt the business; order-book contracts can be adjusted, cancelled or suspended, meaning the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenue.

Process and governance gaps: no independent project appraisal, no monitoring agency, related-party transactions that may continue, and two struck-off promoter companies — all disclosed by the company itself in the risk factors.
